cards.title: Who's in charge?
cards.body:
Right now your music app, your [[browser]] and your messages all want the [[CPU]], a slice of [[RAM]] and a spot on the screen, **all at the same time**.

If they just grabbed what they wanted, they'd crash into each other. Something has to be in charge.

cards.title: The operating system
cards.body:
That something is the **operating system**, or **OS**. It's the main program that starts when you switch a device on, and it runs until you switch it off.

Think of it as a referee:

- It gives each app **turns on the [[CPU]]**, switching between them so fast it looks like they all run at once.
- It **shares out [[RAM]]** and stops apps reading each other's data.
- It talks to the **hardware** (the physical parts: screen, keyboard, Wi-Fi) so apps don't have to.
- It looks after your **files** in [[storage]].

It also installs **updates**, which fix **bugs** (mistakes in a program's instructions) and close **security holes** (weak spots attackers could use). Save your work first, and let an update finish: switching off halfway can leave the OS broken.

cards.prompt: Whose job is it: the **operating system's**, or an **app's**?

items.label: Decide which app uses the CPU next
Share out RAM between open apps
Talk to the keyboard, screen and Wi-Fi
Stop apps reading each other's data
Add a funny filter to a selfie
Add a sticker to a video

cards.explanation: The **OS** manages the shared things every app needs: CPU time, RAM, the hardware and safety. **Apps** do one particular job for you, and ask the OS for what they need.
cards.hint: Think of the OS as the referee. Is this job about sharing something every app needs, or one particular thing an app does for you?
cards.nudge: The OS handles the shared things: CPU turns, RAM, [[hardware]] and keeping apps apart. Apps do one particular job for you.

cards.title: The task manager
cards.body:
Every running program is called a **process**. The OS's **task manager** lists them all, with how much [[CPU]] and [[RAM]] each one uses.

**System processes** are the OS itself: end one and the device crashes or restarts.

If an app freezes, ending its process is the safe fix. You'll lose anything unsaved in it, but nothing else.

cards.prompt: Your laptop has frozen up. Here's its **task manager**. End whatever is hogging the [[CPU]], but **keep your music and your homework [[browser]] open**.
cards.explanation: The **drawing app** was stuck using 85% of the CPU. Ending it freed the CPU, and everything else carried on. Ending **System** would have crashed the whole laptop.
cards.hint: Look at the CPU number for each [[process]]. Which one is taking far more than the rest?
cards.nudge: End only the process hogging the CPU. Never end **System**, and keep your music and browser running.

cards.title: Helpers in the background
cards.body:
Many [[processes|process]] have no window at all. These **background processes** do jobs for you: checking for [[updates|update]], keeping your files matched up with [[the cloud|cloud]] (**syncing**), or scanning for [[viruses|virus]]. Leave security apps running.

Only the OS and security apps can see what's running on your device. A web page can't, so a page that says it "found viruses" is lying.

cards.prompt: You're halfway through an essay on your laptop.

steps.text: A message pops up: **"Updates are ready. Restart now?"**

choices.consequence: The unsaved essay was only in [[RAM]]. Restarting cleared it, and your work is gone.

choices.text: Save the essay first, then restart
choices.consequence: Smart. The essay is safe in [[storage]], and the update can start.
Updates fix [[security holes|security-hole]] that attackers use. Without them, your laptop gets less safe over time.

steps.text: The screen says **"Working on updates. Don't turn off your device."** It's been ten minutes.

choices.text: Hold the power button to stop it
choices.consequence: Cutting an update off halfway can leave the OS broken and unable to start.

choices.text: Plug in the charger and let it finish
choices.consequence: Big updates can take a while. Keeping it powered lets it finish safely.

cards.explanation: **Save your work**, then let updates install. Keep the device plugged in, and never switch it off halfway through. Updates fix [[bugs|bug]] and close security holes.
cards.hint: Think about where unsaved work lives, and what happens to it when a device restarts. Then think about switching off halfway.

cards.prompt: What's the most important reason to install OS [[updates|update]]?

options.text: They fix bugs and security holes
They add more RAM to your device
options.nudge: RAM is hardware, a physical part. An update only changes software, so it can't add more.

options.text: They always make the device faster
options.nudge: Some updates speed things up, but not always. Look for the reason that holds for every update.

options.text: They free up lots of storage
options.nudge: Updates add new code to your device, so they don't usually free up space.

cards.explanation: Updates patch **security holes** and fix bugs. They can't add [[hardware]] like RAM, and they often use a little *more* storage, not less. Some make things faster, but not always.
cards.hint: Think about what an update actually changes: the code, or the physical parts inside your device?

cards.prompt: This laptop has **8 [[GB|gigabyte]] of [[RAM]]**, and it gets slower the longer it's on. Some apps have a **memory leak**: they keep grabbing RAM and never give it back. Move time forward to **at least 40 minutes**, find the leaky app and end it. Keep the **music** playing.
cards.explanation: The **chat app** grew by 0.15 GB every minute. After 40 minutes it was using 6.5 GB and filled RAM on its own. Ending it gives the memory back. Restarting the app (or the laptop) is the everyday fix for a leak until the app's makers fix it.
cards.hint: Slide time forward first, then watch the RAM each app uses. Which one keeps growing when the others stay the same?
cards.nudge: A leaky app's RAM keeps climbing over time. Move time to 40 minutes or more, and don't end the music or **System**.

cards.prompt: You're browsing, and the screen suddenly flashes red.

steps.text: **"WARNING! Your laptop has 5 [[viruses|virus]]! Download CleanerPro now or call this number!"**

choices.consequence: Pop-ups like this are fakes. The "cleaner" is usually the harmful program itself.
It's a scam. The caller will ask for money or for control of your laptop.

choices.text: Don't click anything in it. Close the tab
choices.consequence: Good instinct. A web page can't scan your laptop, so this warning is fake.

steps.text: The page keeps popping back up and the tab won't close.

choices.text: End the browser in the task manager and tell an adult
choices.consequence: The page is gone, and an adult can help you check everything is fine.
Buttons on a fake pop-up can do anything, including start a download.

cards.explanation: A web page can't see what's on your laptop, so a pop-up claiming to have found viruses is **fake**. Don't click anything inside it. Close the browser (using the task manager if you need to) and tell an adult.
cards.hint: Can a web page really see what's on your laptop? Think about who can, and whether you should click anything it shows you.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- The **operating system** is the referee. It shares out the [[CPU]] and [[RAM]], talks to the [[hardware]] and looks after files.
- The **task manager** shows every **process**, including background and system ones.
- End a frozen app's process to fix it, but never a [[system process]].
- **Save your work**, then let [[updates|update]] finish.

Next: where your files actually live.
